samples.text:
Rich countries often give money to poor countries to help them. This essay will explain the reasons why they do this and which kind of help I think is the most effective in the long term.

There are several reasons for giving financial aid. The first reason is humanitarian. When there is a natural disaster like an earthquake or a flood, people in poor countries need food, water and medicine urgently, and rich countries want to help them because it is right thing to do. Secondly, wealthy countries also get benefits from giving aid. For example, they can build good relationship with the other country and later they can do business or trade with it. Also, some rich countries give aid because they want to have political influence in that region.

In my opinion, the most effective help in the long term is not only giving money but helping poor countries to develop themselves. Money can be spent quickly or can be stolen by corrupt officials, so the problem continue. Instead, rich countries should invest in education and training, so that people can get better jobs and earn their own money. For instance, building schools and training teachers will help a whole generation. Also, they can help to build infrastructure like roads, hospitals and clean water system, and share their technology with local farmers so they can grow more food.

In conclusion, wealthy countries give aid because they want to help people and also for their own economic and political benefits. I believe that education, infrastructure and technology is more useful than just money, because it helps poor countries to become independent in the future.
samples.why: Both questions answered with a clear opinion · reasons relevant but briefly explained · simple linking (Secondly, Also, For instance) · adequate vocabulary · errors in articles and subject-verb agreement that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
Wealthy nations commonly provide financial assistance to less developed countries. This essay will explore the motives behind such aid and argue that support which builds long-term capacity, particularly in education and infrastructure, is more effective than direct financial transfers.

Wealthy countries give aid for a combination of moral and practical reasons. The most obvious motive is humanitarian: when poorer nations are affected by famine, conflict or natural disasters, there is a strong ethical case for helping those in need, and public opinion in donor countries usually approves. However, aid is also a tool of foreign policy. By supporting a developing country, a donor can strengthen diplomatic ties and gain influence in a strategically important region. There are economic motives as well, since growth in poorer countries can create new markets for the donor's exports, and some aid is even tied to the purchase of goods or services from the donor nation. Finally, reducing poverty abroad may help to limit global problems such as the spread of disease.

As for long-term results, I believe aid which helps countries to become self-sufficient is the most valuable. Emergency funding is essential in a crisis, but continuous cash transfers can create dependency and are sometimes lost through corruption. By contrast, investment in education equips people with skills they can use for decades, and support for healthcare produces a healthier, more productive workforce. Projects such as roads, electricity networks and irrigation systems enable local businesses and farmers to increase their output and reach new markets. Such help works best when it is designed in partnership with local communities, so that projects meet genuine needs and is maintained after foreign experts leave.

In conclusion, wealthy countries give aid out of humanitarian concern as well as political and economic self-interest. In the long run, assistance that develops education, health and infrastructure is far more effective than simply providing money.
samples.why: Clear position with both questions answered and developed · logical progression from motives to solutions · good range of vocabulary (self-sufficient, diplomatic ties, dependency) · mostly accurate with one agreement slip.

samples.text:
Financial aid from wealthy to poorer nations is a long-established feature of international relations, yet the reasons behind it are rarely purely altruistic, and the forms it takes vary greatly in their lasting impact. In my view, aid that strengthens a country's own capacity to generate wealth and provide services is by far the most effective over time.

The motives of donor countries are typically a blend of principle and self-interest. On a moral level, there is a widely shared sense that prosperous nations have an obligation to relieve suffering, particularly in the aftermath of disasters or during famines. At the same time, aid serves diplomatic ends. Supporting a developing country can secure its goodwill, strengthen alliances and extend a donor's influence in regions of strategic importance. Economic calculation also plays a role: a more prosperous partner becomes a larger market for exports and a more stable place to invest, and some aid is explicitly tied to contracts for the donor's own firms. Lastly, since epidemics and instability rarely respect borders, reducing poverty abroad can serve donors' own security.

When it comes to long-term effectiveness, the crucial distinction is between assistance that meets immediate needs and assistance that builds lasting capability. Emergency relief is indispensable in a crisis, but sustained cash transfers to governments risk fostering dependency and can be diverted by corruption. Investment in education, by contrast, pays dividends for generations, while support for primary healthcare raises productivity as well as wellbeing. Infrastructure such as reliable electricity, roads and irrigation enables farmers and entrepreneurs to expand, creating employment that no donation could sustain. These projects are most successful when shaped by local communities, which ensures that they reflect genuine priorities and continue once foreign involvement ends.

In conclusion, wealthy countries give aid out of a mixture of compassion, diplomacy and economic interest. The most effective long-term help is not money alone but investment in the education, health and infrastructure that allow poorer nations to prosper independently.
samples.why: Both questions answered with a sophisticated, clearly argued position · ideas extended and logically organised · precise, wide-ranging vocabulary (altruistic, diverted, pays dividends) · varied complex structures, error-free.
